Hook to Cook

By: Liz Fish | Production

Proposal


Show:

Unique Selling Point:
Finally eating local fish can be done with a clean conscience without worrying whether the fish you are eating is having a disastrous impact on the ocean, or if it’s travelled across the continent to reach your plate. A series of Smartphone apps are changing artisanal fishermen’s lives, enabling them to sell fish to restaurants that is not only locally caught, but also fully traceable. This direct access to the restaurants is disrupting the supply chain and putting money directly into the pockets of subsistence fishermen. It’s making sustainably, traceable fish a reality in 22 restaurants across the Western Cape.

Its a good news fishing story where fishermen are succeeding in an environment where most fishing stories are negative and its only the big players that are succeeding. Technology on smartphones is empowering the small guys

Summary:
Abalobe is an organisation that is enabling subsistence fishermen to get organised, access local markets, and keep track of fish stocks and their own finances on their smartphones. It also allows customers to learn more about the fish they are eating and about the life of the person who caught it through a QR code (two-dimensional barcode) which they access when their plate of fish is served. And the process gives fisheries researchers access to a host of local data. This app has value for fishermen, fishing co-operatives, monitors, fishing managers and seafood retailers.

One of the biggest advantages of this app is that chefs are now offering a far wider range of fish on their menus - fish like Black bream, locally known as “Hottentot” is now being sold in top-end restaurants like Catharina’s on the Steenberg Wine Estate in Contantia. It’s taking the pressure off well-known fish and creating a market for fish that were previously seen as low-value. David Shoshola, a 3rd generation Lamberts Bay fisherman, says that it’s taken the pressure off the high value catches like crayfish. Crayfish licences are becoming extremely difficult to access and are closely linked with crime syndicates. David can now sell fish like Black bream - previously only marketable in the village for very little - at the same price as yellowtail. For the first time in years he doesn’t care that he doesn’t have a crayfish licence because he can sell fish throughout the year at a consistent price.

The most important app for fishermen is the “dashboard”: here they log exactly what was caught, how many fish, how much it was sold for, weather conditions, who caught it and who bought it, what the cost of petrol was, and what they earned. This data has many spin offs.


Further information:
There are roughly 30 000 artisanal fishermen and they have always lived off a cash economy with no record-keeping now they have a record of their expenses and their income, proof of how many people they employ, and are now “seen” by financial institution as they have documented proof of their income. Despite having created employment for those around them for years, they are now traceable financially and have financial records that go back several years.

This data is also critical for fisheries research feeding into catch allowances, stocks, quotas and monitoring and for a host of marine resource researchers. It’s conservation with fishermen rather than against them. This information is also feeding into Climate change research about local fish stocks and changing migratory patterns. Institutions like the WWF’s Sustainable Seafood Initiative to reflect accurately the state of various fish stocks. For example, fewer snoek have been caught this year in Lamberts Bay than last year, but the price is better this year, and this data was gathered at no cost to any institution.

Fishermen are also able to assist each other and co-operate, pooling their catches and sharing the costs of getting them to the market. To date, 22 restaurants across the Western Cape now buy directly from the fishermen, and the chefs say the quality of the fish is exceptional. The price is the same as from the wholesalers and they are now able to offer a far wider range of dishes to their clients. The fishermen are amazed that their humble “Hottenot” is being turned into sophisticated paté and sushi.

The piece will be visually beautiful - out on the water in the early morning; fish being caught on a hand line, cleaned by local women; then served in the beautiful world-class restaurants in the Constantia valley by world class chefs like Archie Maclean at Catharina’s Restaurant or Kerry Kilpin at Steenberg’s Bistro 1682, or La Tete in Bree Street. These chefs say their fish sales have soared and they are loving the fact that it’s lowering their carbon footprint and making a real social impact in communities that are struggling to survive.

Subsistence fishing has been the backbone of coastal villages along the Western Cape coastline for centuries, but over the years, lack of access to markets and fishing quotas have left them increasing marginalised and impoverished. This app has the potential to change that, and 200 fishermen who are using the app are beginning to feel the impact as their lives stabilise. It’s giving them a voice, and a direct line of communication with fisheries research and financial institutions.

Press Release:


Hook to Cook
A series of smartphone apps are disrupting traditional supply chain systems and changing the lives of artisanal fishermen. By enabling them to sell fish to restaurants without the middleman, these apps are putting money directly into the pockets of subsistence fishermen.


Script:


Script: Romantic fishing villages like Lamberts bay along the Cape West Coast, with scenes of fishermen going out to sea early in the morning, belie the extreme poverty that these families are trapped in. David Shoshola has been a fisherman living a hand to mouth existence all his life.
David “When the snoek are running, everybody works at the harbour, not just the fishermen who catch the fish, there is an income for many families. The fishermen that gets up at 4 in the morning to make it possible - at the end of the day when the snoek are gone and there is nothing left in the water that we can catch, then they also have nothing. You are a nobody, you don’t have a pay slip, I can say to you that nowadays from the snoek for a month I got R15 000, but I can’t show it. If I say to someone I am a fisherman , you can’t prove it, fishermen are valued low, I don’t have a pay slip so it’s just a story.
Link: Fishermen risk their lives going to sea and are seldom compensated for the true costs involved in catching that fish because the buyers determine the price.
Script: And ironically the more fish they land, the lower the per kilo price. But a new mobile app known as Abalobi - small scale fisher in isiXhosa, is changing all that.
David “I could never have dreamed as a fisher that always just off-loaded my product, received cash for it and gone home and given my wife the money, and tomorrow morning off to sea again, it’s no longer that day-to-day life, there is now a bigger picture and suddenly I see that I am on a road to somewhere”
Script: Serge Raemaekers was the visionary behind Abalobi mobile apps
Serge “ Yeah I've always been passionate about the marine environment and started off looking at marine biology and when I came to South Africa about 14 years ago I dive more in the social part of fisheries research fisheries management
Script: During his fisheries research at UCT, Serge was stuck by the wealth of indigenous knowledge artisanal fishermen have, but they are marginalised when it comes to decisions around quotas and fish stocks
Serge “I think it's fair to say that the overall level fishers feel very disempowered, when they sit at the decision making table or to even try and sit at the decision making table with the fisheries authority.
Script: Abalobi started in 2015, initially just establishing networks with small scale fishers and eventually they co-designed a mobile app with the fishermen. Currently there are over 300 fishermen using the app in various ways.
David “Let’s start at the beginning, you register on the Abalobi app and you use the Abalobi app to capture your data… it’s the diary of a fisher, You go to sea, you catch fish and you record it, before you used an ordinary pen and paper -it can get wet your book can get lost. We put it on our smart phone and we can go back and look how was the season.
Script: Fishers are generally poorly educated, and so involving them in designing the app has been critical, explains Nico Waldeck, director of community engagement.
Nico “They don’t like to write, click we want to see photos, and then we can just press on it and that is why the app is so easy for them to use because they said this is how it must work…., and the old guys with the fat fingers and they struggled a bit, but when they mastered the click the fishers began to enjoy it
Serge “So we have a few different apps that work for different stakeholders. We have a monitoring app that works for the fisheries authorities for the extension officers out there in harbours to record fishing activities to sample the fish. We have the fisher app which is the main app that allows fishers to record their own activities manage their balance sheet and post their catch on the Abalobi marketplace. And then we have the Abaloni marketplace which really allows that connection between the Chefs and these groups of fishers to access that catch of the day hat storied seafood
Link: The Abalobi app is the uber of the fish markets it disrupting the traditional supply chain, enabling marginalised fishermen to access top Cape Town restaurants directly and to be paid a fair price for their catch.
Script: Bistro 1682 was the first restaurant to start ordering off the Abalobi Market app, which Chef Penny Garrord says has tripled their fish sales
Claire “How does the Abalobi work?
Penny “ We get information on the app, they let us know when the boats are going out and as they come in they upload all information on the app as to what fish they caught and how much fish they have caught. And from there we are then able to order as much as we want
Serge “So this is where Abalobi I suppose is Business Unusual. We're working with these chefs not to allow them to order on the market place those three four species that everybody knows but we're working with these chefs say this is the catch of the day. Today the sea has to offer this now chef work with it
Link: Chefs are usually forced to cook what their clients know and that causes a lot of pressure on the same fish. But 22 restaurants in the Western Cape are breaking with that tradition and serving their clients a whole range of sustainable fish
Penny “So this is the Cape Bream. You can see it is so incredible the flesh is so firm. 2:49:53] and you can the eyes are so glossy. We are receiving a whole lot of different types of fish that we are able to serve and educate people about and this is also nice for our kitchen to be able to see all the different types of fish that we have in our ocean that a people haven't seen before or have little knowledge of
Claire “And price how does that compare to other supplies
Penny. “We are paying pretty much the same thing. The thing about Abalobi we know that what we are paying for is going direct to the fishermen and they are getting their worth for what we are receiving.
Script: Wilfred Consalves had a good day
Wilfred “The profit we made was R3129. The price is also very different, we have 10 fishers in a bunch and we sell it for R50 a bunch, by the restaurant you get R60 a kilo, it’s about R120 for a bunch that I used to get R50 for
Script: The question is, will things get ugly by taking out the buyers and disrupting the supply chain
Nico “so at this stage there is no negative connotation with what we are doing - the people we are working with at the moment are the small boats that are selling direct to the chefs so there is fish for everyone in this process
Script: The market mobile app has only been operating for six months but Wilfred can already feel the impact
Wilfred “I had a problem with my motors, and there weren’t times that I could put money away, because the money you make every day you can’t put that aside. Now I can put my money away, and anyway you don’t have to do it yourself, because if I offload fish at the Chef, the money goes straight into my account.
Serge “So we've built this digital value chain that allows Fishers to connect with the market. But it also allows the market to pay the fishes directly to their bank account. So the chef pays with his or her credit card or instant eft and depending on who contributes to the order whether it's one Fisher or five fishes they get paid straightaway.
Script: David says for the first time he can survive without a crayfish quota, because he is able to sell a range of fish that have always been considered of low value
David “ In December we catch crayfish, good crayfish, we earn money and send our children to school the following year, pay all the school fees all I did this with crayfish money. This year I couldn’t manage this because of politics, but with the Cape Bream, R60 a kilo I could send my children to school. So suddenly I don’t have to concentrate on crayfish that has a high value, but on fishing as a whole that doesn’t have lots of politics in it, and very important the Cape Bream is green on the SASSI list.
Script: Because the fishermen are at sea all the time, their data makes an invaluable contribution to scientific research and conservation.
Nico “This is what we call real time data so if there is a crisis somewhere in the fishing industry, any manager from Fisheries can have access to this data, if the fishers agree to it, they can see what is the problem and they can immediately make a decision. But this data can also empower David to speak to researchers, so other people don’t talk on behalf of the fishermen, they can speak for themselves.
Link: When we are presented with a delicious plate of fish we seldom think about who caught it and how it got to our table. And if we order the catch of the day we don’t really know if in fact just that, it could have come from anywhere across the continent.
Penny: “So every day load of fish that we receive each batch of fish has a QR code connected to the fishermen that has caught that batch so we can sometimes get three different fishermen that have caught our fish and each fisherman or each fish has its own QR code which the guests can connect to and see Wilfred or David or whoever has caught it.
Script “Natalie Wells says they are now serving fish that hasn’t been on offer for the last 10 years, and the clients are fascinated to learn about it, and more importantly who caught it.
Natalie Wells: When you scan the QR code all the information will come up the fisherman that caught your fish where it was fish exactly what fish is caught some information on the fish so you can see exactly where your fish came from
Vox Marc Viakovsky “It makes an impact on somebodies life”
Jan Sluis-Cremer” it’s not just some fishing trawler out there that’s put a net in the sea and just dragging everything with it you kind of know where your meal is coming from
Serge “It allows fishing communities’ fisheries along the South African coast to promote their low impact methods. These fisheries go out on day trips they fish with hand line and they generally fish with very responsible low impact methods. We need to be able to promote to a particular market
David “I could never have dreamed that I could get my Cape Bream straight to a restaurant. What we know is not street stories or fishermen’s tales, it is what we see and it’s what we know and we are on the right road.

And if we order the catch of the day we don’t really know if in fact just that, it could have come from anywhere across the continent. Penny: “So every day load of fish that we receive each batch of fish has a QR code connected to the fishermen that has caught that batch so we can sometimes get three different fishermen that have caught our fish and each fisherman or each fish has its own QR code which the guests can connect to and see Wilfred or David or whoever has caught it. Script “Natalie Wells says they are now serving fish that hasn’t been on offer for the last 10 years, and the clients are fascinated to learn about it, and more importantly who caught it. Natalie Wells: When you scan the QR code all the information will come up the fisherman that caught your fish where it was fish exactly what fish is caught some information on the fish so you can see exactly where your fish came from Vox Marc Viakovsky “It makes an impact on somebodies life” Jan Sluis-Cremer” it’s not just some fishing trawler out there that’s put a net in the sea and just dragging everything with it you kind of know where your meal is coming from Serge “It allows fishing communities’ fisheries along the South African coast to promote their low impact methods. These fisheries go out on day trips they fish with hand line and they generally fish with very responsible low impact methods. We need to be able to promote to a particular market David “I could never have dreamed that I could get my Cape Bream straight to a restaurant. What we know is not street stories or fishermen’s tales, it is what we see and it’s what we know and we are on the right road. metadata.Unique Selling Point: Finally eating local fish can be done with a clean conscience without worrying whether the fish you are eating is having a disastrous impact on the ocean, or if it’s travelled across the continent to reach your plate. A series of Smartphone apps are changing artisanal fishermen’s lives, enabling them to sell fish to restaurants that is not only locally caught, but also fully traceable. This direct access to the restaurants is disrupting the supply chain and putting money directly into the pockets of subsistence fishermen. It’s making sustainably, traceable fish a reality in 22 restaurants across the Western Cape. Its a good news fishing story where fishermen are succeeding in an environment where most fishing stories are negative and its only the big players that are succeeding. Technology on smartphones is empowering the small guys
metadata.Summary: Abalobe is an organisation that is enabling subsistence fishermen to get organised, access local markets, and keep track of fish stocks and their own finances on their smartphones. It also allows customers to learn more about the fish they are eating and about the life of the person who caught it through a QR code (two-dimensional barcode) which they access when their plate of fish is served. And the process gives fisheries researchers access to a host of local data. This app has value for fishermen, fishing co-operatives, monitors, fishing managers and seafood retailers. One of the biggest advantages of this app is that chefs are now offering a far wider range of fish on their menus - fish like Black bream, locally known as “Hottentot” is now being sold in top-end restaurants like Catharina’s on the Steenberg Wine Estate in Contantia. It’s taking the pressure off well-known fish and creating a market for fish that were previously seen as low-value. David Shoshola, a 3rd generation Lamberts Bay fisherman, says that it’s taken the pressure off the high value catches like crayfish. Crayfish licences are becoming extremely difficult to access and are closely linked with crime syndicates. David can now sell fish like Black bream - previously only marketable in the village for very little - at the same price as yellowtail. For the first time in years he doesn’t care that he doesn’t have a crayfish licence because he can sell fish throughout the year at a consistent price. The most important app for fishermen is the “dashboard”: here they log exactly what was caught, how many fish, how much it was sold for, weather conditions, who caught it and who bought it, what the cost of petrol was, and what they earned. This data has many spin offs.
metadata.Further information: There are roughly 30 000 artisanal fishermen and they have always lived off a cash economy with no record-keeping now they have a record of their expenses and their income, proof of how many people they employ, and are now “seen” by financial institution as they have documented proof of their income. Despite having created employment for those around them for years, they are now traceable financially and have financial records that go back several years. This data is also critical for fisheries research feeding into catch allowances, stocks, quotas and monitoring and for a host of marine resource researchers. It’s conservation with fishermen rather than against them. This information is also feeding into Climate change research about local fish stocks and changing migratory patterns. Institutions like the WWF’s Sustainable Seafood Initiative to reflect accurately the state of various fish stocks. For example, fewer snoek have been caught this year in Lamberts Bay than last year, but the price is better this year, and this data was gathered at no cost to any institution. Fishermen are also able to assist each other and co-operate, pooling their catches and sharing the costs of getting them to the market. To date, 22 restaurants across the Western Cape now buy directly from the fishermen, and the chefs say the quality of the fish is exceptional. The price is the same as from the wholesalers and they are now able to offer a far wider range of dishes to their clients. The fishermen are amazed that their humble “Hottenot” is being turned into sophisticated paté and sushi. The piece will be visually beautiful - out on the water in the early morning; fish being caught on a hand line, cleaned by local women; then served in the beautiful world-class restaurants in the Constantia valley by world class chefs like Archie Maclean at Catharina’s Restaurant or Kerry Kilpin at Steenberg’s Bistro 1682, or La Tete in Bree Street. These chefs say their fish sales have soared and they are loving the fact that it’s lowering their carbon footprint and making a real social impact in communities that are struggling to survive. Subsistence fishing has been the backbone of coastal villages along the Western Cape coastline for centuries, but over the years, lack of access to markets and fishing quotas have left them increasing marginalised and impoverished. This app has the potential to change that, and 200 fishermen who are using the app are beginning to feel the impact as their lives stabilise. It’s giving them a voice, and a direct line of communication with fisheries research and financial institutions.
